title: Dead-Letter Queue Fundamentals
description: Understand what dead-letter queues are, why they matter, and how major brokers like RabbitMQ and AWS SQS implement them.

data.text: A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a special queue where message brokers send messages that cannot be processed successfully. Instead of losing these messages forever, the broker routes them to a separate destination so engineers can investigate, fix, and replay them later.

Distributed systems fail. Networks blip, databases lock, and third-party APIs time out. Without a DLQ, failed messages simply disappear or block the queue indefinitely. A DLQ keeps the main queue flowing while preserving failed work for later inspection. This separation prevents bad messages from poisoning consumers and makes recovery predictable.

data.title: Operational Benefit
data.text: DLQs turn silent message loss into a visible, recoverable workflow. Teams can fix the root cause and replay messages without restarting the entire system.

RabbitMQ uses a dead-letter exchange (DLX). When a message is rejected, expires, or the queue overflows, the broker republishes it to the configured DLX, which routes it to a DLQ. AWS SQS uses a redrive policy. When a message exceeds the maximum receive count, SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue automatically.
